title: Managing Long-Running Tasks
summary: Acknowledge quickly, do the work in the background, and make progress observable.
keyPoints: Move work to the background when its duration is unpredictable or exceeds the request budget.
Persist a job record before acknowledging; return 202 with a job ID and status URL.
Workers claim jobs with leases and must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.
Retry transient failures with backoff and jitter, then send exhausted jobs to a dead-letter queue.
Scale workers on queue depth and oldest-job age, and bound the queue with load shedding.
Keep short, predictable work synchronous; a queue adds real operational cost.

complexity.note: Return 202 only after the job is persisted.
A lease lets another worker recover a crashed job.
Update every few seconds or percent, not every item.
Cap attempts and classify permanent failures.
Needs an owner, an alert, and a replay tool.

commonMistakes: Running a multi-minute task inside the request and hoping the gateway timeout is generous enough.
Retrying a permanent failure such as an invalid file format until the queue fills.
Scaling workers on CPU while the queue grows because workers are waiting on a remote service.
Promising exactly-once processing instead of at-least-once delivery with idempotent outputs.
interviewNotes: State the request budget and why the task cannot fit inside it.
Show the job record, the 202 response, and the status endpoint.
Explain the lease and what happens when a worker dies mid-job.
Separate transient failures from permanent ones, and name the dead-letter policy.
Say how cancellation works and whether the partial output is kept or removed.

checkYourself.question: Why return 202 instead of 200 after submitting a job?
checkYourself.answer: 202 means the request was accepted for processing but has not completed. It matches the truth: the job exists, and the client should poll or subscribe for the result.

checkYourself.question: How does a worker lease help after a crash?
checkYourself.answer: The lease expires if the worker stops heartbeating. Another worker can then claim the job and finish the work, instead of leaving it stuck forever.

checkYourself.question: Why is a dead-letter queue not a trash can?
checkYourself.answer: It holds jobs that need inspection, repair, and replay. Without an owner and a process, failures accumulate silently and users never receive their results.
